title: Opus modelled this pocket watch from a single photo, as code, so every part is controllable
author: Nehekhara

comments.author: Top_Issue_7032
comments.body: Fantastic! Do you mind me asking how you pulled this off?

replies.author: Nehekhara
replies.body:
Opus in Claude Code, driving a toolkit I wrote called antics-modelkit.  
  
`npm i antics-modelkit three`  
  
It's three.js underneath and runs headless in Node, so there's no modelling app anywhere in the loop. Opus writes a file that returns the named parts, then the build checks the geometry and spits out a .glb.  
  
A text prompt on its own works fine, but you get a lot more detail out of it if you give it an image to work from.  
  
If you give it a go I'd love to hear how you get on!

replies.author: Nehekhara
replies.body:
Godot's fine and you won't need any C# bindings. The kit isn't a runtime library, it's a build step. It runs in Node on your machine and what comes out is a plain .glb, which Godot imports like any other asset. Nothing from the kit ships with your game, so the language it's written in never reaches you.

Named parts come through as named nodes in the imported scene, so you can still grab them from C# and move them around.

One thing worth checking before you spend time on it: the exporter quantises meshes and marks that as a required glTF extension, and I've only tested imports in three.js and Blender. You can grab any .glb from the website and drop it into Godot. If it fails let me know and I'll add a flag to turn quantisation off.

On the docs, that page is just the overview. And no, you don't write box or sit yourself, those come from the package. The snippet is the file you write using them.

Really though, you're not meant to write it by hand. Point your agent at this:

`Read` [`https://antics.gg/models/llms.txt`](https://antics.gg/models/llms.txt)`, then build me a [thing] with antics-modelkit and export it as a .glb`

Then run `npx modelkit build` and you've got a file to import.

Good point on the instructions though, they're not clear enough. I'll fix that!

replies.author: Old_Swan8945
replies.body: Can I ask how that framework works that you created? How long did this take you to build?

replies.author: Nehekhara
replies.body:
You describe a profile and sweep it rather than placing primitives. Most things are either spun round an axis (the watch case, a bottle, a column) or run along a curve (a rail, a limb). A model is a file exporting one function per asset returning named parts, then `npx modelkit build` validates the geometry and writes the .glb.  
  
It checks for surfaces built inside out, holes you can see into, parts left floating without touching anything, two surfaces fighting over the same spot, whether the model still reads at the size it'll actually be drawn, etc. The output also goes through the official glTF validator, so a file that builds isn't quietly malformed.  
  
The point is to cut down how many times you go round the screenshot, describe it, fix it loop. The build catches the mechanical problems so you only spend your own eyes on whether it looks right.  
  
Started about two weeks ago and not really as a project. I kept hitting the same problems making models for my own games, so I built this.

replies.author: Old_Swan8945
replies.body:
That's super cool because Watchers are such complicated objects and to be able to put one together using code is actually quite incredible.

 The best I've been able to do is buildings. But I've been finding very similar things to you where finding the right way to describe the object is incredibly important. What's the right basis function or what are the right axes on which you can parameterize the object?

 

https://preview.redd.it/2hk5ztk40lih1.png?width=900&format=png&auto=webp&s=9a75cd015b015d140ff8b4cf377b5d8584e88a35

replies.author: Nehekhara
replies.body:
Yes, that's the whole game. I could already see that house used in a game.

  
What worked for me is picking the one dimension the object is really about and making everything else a fraction of it. On the watch that's the case diameter, so the bezel, the dial, the hand lengths and the movement are all expressed against it. Change that number and it stays a watch instead of becoming a dinner plate.  
  
The mistake I made more than any other is scaling something off the wrong dimension. Buildings are full of those. I had a roof eave curving up by a fraction of the building's depth, when it should have been a fraction of how far the roof drops. It looks perfectly reasonable in the code and you only catch it in a render.  
  
  
So the rule I ended up with: whatever you scale off should belong to the same part of the object as the thing you're calculating. An eave lift scaled off how far the roof drops is fine. Scaled off the building's overall depth, it only looks right at the one size you happened to be testing, and it drifts the moment you change anything.  
  
  
This [shophouse](http://antics.gg/m/shophouse-270bca) was made using this tool, and the recipe's on the page.
